question_text: A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because his wife has noticed that his left eye looks smaller than his right. He has had worsening left shoulder and arm pain for 3 months. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Examination shows left-sided ptosis. The pupils are unequal but reactive to light; when measured in dim light, the left pupil is 3 mm and the right pupil is 5 mm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's ophthalmologic symptoms?

                    ### Question
                    A 60-year-old man comes to the physician because his wife has noticed that his left eye looks smaller than his right. He has had worsening left shoulder and arm pain for 3 months. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 35 years. Examination shows left-sided ptosis. The pupils are unequal but reactive to light; when measured in dim light, the left pupil is 3 mm and the right pupil is 5 mm. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's ophthalmologic symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Thrombosis of the cavernous sinus
opb. Aneurysm of the posterior cerebral artery
opc. Dissection of the carotid artery
opd. Compression of the stellate ganglion
ope. Infiltration of the cervical plexus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The most likely cause of this patient's ophthalmologic symptoms is compression of the stellate ganglion, possibly due to smoking-related vascular diseases leading to Horner syndrome. The presence of ptosis and miosis supports this conclusion, with the unequal pupils suggesting anisocoria related to sympathetic dysfunction rather than carotid artery dissection or other causes.
